vignette: Nguyen is a 27-year-old South Eastern Asian male and a journalist. He has been in a relationship for several years but recently experienced severe physical abuse at the hands of his romantic partner. The traumatic event itself was a pivotal moment that marked the beginning of Nguyen's struggle with PTSD symptoms, which have significantly impacted his daily life. The night of the incident remains vivid in Nguyen's mind. His partner had become increasingly agitated after a heated argument over their work schedules and personal responsibilities. The argument escalated into physical violence, leaving Nguyen severely shaken both physically and emotionally. Since then, simple triggers like being on public transport, especially buses, have become sources of immense anxiety for him. He often feels on edge when riding the bus to his office or to meet clients for interviews, constantly vigilant and expecting something bad to happen. Nguyen also finds himself avoiding situations where he has to be alone with men. This avoidance extends beyond just his immediate surroundings; it influences his work and relationships. As a journalist, Nguyen has started to decline assignments that require him to interview male sources one-on-one or travel solo to meet contacts in unfamiliar areas. He often rationalizes these decisions by telling himself that it's better to be cautious, even though he knows this is affecting the scope of his reporting. Nguyen dwells on what he believes he did wrong, constantly questioning whether he could have prevented the abuse if only he had acted differently. This self-blame is compounded by his tendency to suppress any feelings of anger. He never allows himself to feel or express anger, instead channeling his emotions into undereating and restricting food as a way of coping with the overwhelming sense of guilt and inadequacy. Nguyen's nights are often restless, filled with waking up multiple times to check whether he is safe, convinced that something bad is about to happen. Even when others assure him that everything is fine, he finds it impossible to believe them, unable to trust in his own safety or the intentions of those around him. When the memory of the traumatic event surfaces, it feels like it's happening all over again, overwhelming him with a flood of emotions and physical pain in the same areas where he was hurt. Nguyen has come to fear that harm can come from anyone, anywhere, at any time, and this constant vigilance is exhausting. He mistrusts people easily, even those close to him, feeling inadequate and vulnerable. His partner's betrayal has left deep scars, not just on his body but also on his psyche. Nguyen's relationship with his partner has suffered as a result of these symptoms. They have frequent arguments about his need for constant vigilance and his reluctance to trust anyone, including his partner. Nguyen is aware that his behavior affects their relationship negatively, but he cannot seem to break free from the cycle of fear and mistrust. What finally brought Nguyen to seek help was a particularly difficult incident where he broke down during a routine bus ride home after work. He felt overwhelmed by the memories and physical sensations, which left him unable to function properly at his job or in his personal life. Nguyen is most afraid that he will never be able to trust anyone again and that the trauma will continue to control his life. However, he also holds hope for recovery, hoping that with help, he can regain a sense of safety and trust in himself and others. Nguyen's journey towards healing begins with recognizing these symptoms as manifestations of PTSD rather than personal failures. He hopes that through therapy, he can learn strategies to cope with triggers, rebuild his trust, and regain control over his life without the constant fear of impending harm.
